## The defect

`publish-pytest` → **Verify pinned npm release is published** asked npm
exactly once, so it raced the registry.

On the v1.41.0 release (run
[34546620094](https://github.com/CopilotKit/aimock/actions/runs/34546620094)):

- `publish` published `@copilotkit/aimock@1.41.0` at `00:30:31`
- `publish-pytest` queried npm at `00:30:49` — **18 seconds later**
- npm answered `E404 No match found for version 1.41.0`
- the step exited 1 and the whole Release run went red

The version existed. Re-running the failed job unchanged passed and
published nothing. It will fail on roughly any release where propagation
is slow, and it makes a completely successful release look broken.

## The fix

Poll to a deadline instead of asking once. The guard is unchanged in
purpose: it still exists to stop aimock-pytest shipping a pin to a
version that was never published, and it still fails when the version is
genuinely absent.

**Ceiling: 300s**, backoff 5s doubling to a 30s cap (~13 attempts). 300s
is ~16x the observed 18s lag and past npm's replication tail, while
staying small beside this job's own checkout/setup. A pin still missing
after five minutes is a bad pin, not propagation, and must go red.

**Transient vs. genuine.** A per-version `E404` conflates two failures,
so a companion `npm view <pkg> versions --json` splits them:

| companion query | meaning | action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the **package** itself 404s | a bad pin — never propagation | **fail
immediately**, don't wait 5 minutes |
| the version list **already carries** the version | published; the
per-version 404 was a stale packument | **accept** — the registry has
already proven the fact |
| package exists, version absent | genuinely ambiguous | keep waiting;
this is what the deadline is for |
| package query fails **without** a 404 | registry unreachable |
transient, keep waiting |

Every attempt logs its timestamp, the attempt number, and the npm error
it got, so a future failure is diagnosable from the run log rather than
a bare exit 1.

## Red → green

The step's own `run:` body was extracted verbatim and executed.

### RED (body on `main` @ `42eaaa2`)

npm error code E404
npm error 404 No match found for version 99.99.99
RED-1 exit=1 elapsed=0s
```

The race shape — a stub that 404s on the first 2 calls then succeeds:

```

```

One call, zero wait, red — where call 3 would have succeeded. That is
the production failure exactly.

### GREEN — the transient case now survives

attempt 1 (t+0s): @copilotkit/aimock@1.41.0 not visible yet
  | npm error 404 No match found for version 1.41.0
  @copilotkit/aimock exists but does not list 1.41.0 yet - lag or a bad pin, still waiting
  retrying in 1s
attempt 2 (t+2s): @copilotkit/aimock@1.41.0 not visible yet
  retrying in 1s
attempt 3: @copilotkit/aimock@1.41.0 is published (1.41.0)
GREEN-A exit=0 elapsed=3s calls=3
```

### GREEN — the half that actually matters: a genuinely missing version
still FAILS

Full **default** 300s window, **real npm**, `99.99.99`:

```
::error::@copilotkit/aimock@99.99.99 is still not published after 13 attempts over 323s

packages/aimock-pytest/src/aimock_pytest/_version.py; refusing to publish a pin to a
version npm does not have.

exit=1  elapsed=323s  attempts=13

And a pin to a package that does not exist fails **fast**, without

::error::npm has no package named @copilotkit/aimock at all, so the pin 1.41.0 in
packages/aimock-pytest/src/aimock_pytest/_version.py is not a propagation delay.

feat(control-api): journal filters, fixtures dump, and runtime chaos control

fix(control-api): scope chaos per test id, validate journal params, fix dump kinds

Follow-up fixes on this PR's new control surface, before it becomes a
permanent public contract.

- Runtime chaos is now scoped to the caller's X-Test-Id, like every other
  mutable axis in the server (fixture match-counts, video job maps). A
  global switch is unusable under the topology aimock is built for: one
  shared process serving a parallel suite, where one test enabling chaos
  failed every test running beside it. Scoping is by header on both sides
  -- the control call and the traffic it affects -- so the two can never
  resolve to different scopes.
- POST /__aimock/reset now drops every chaos override, restoring the
  config the server was STARTED with. Reset is the isolation barrier a
  parallel harness leans on; chaos escaping it produced 500s that look
  like application bugs. This also fixes the in-process LLMock.reset().
- The override no longer latches: a server started with --chaos-drop was
  permanently destroyed by the first empty body, with no way back. Added
  DELETE /__aimock/chaos to drop one override without a full reset.
- PUT -> POST. PUT would have been the only one in the whole control
  surface (everything else is GET/POST/DELETE) and it was missing from
  Access-Control-Allow-Methods, so the preflight blocked browser
  harnesses. POST needs no new CORS method.
- Unknown journal query params are now 400 instead of silently returning
  the whole journal -- matching the 'include' validation this PR already
  had two routes down. ?statusCode=404 used to pass vacuously forever.
- The testId filter no longer prefix-collides (?testId=t1 matched t10);
  it resolves each entry the way the server resolves a request.
- fixtureResponseKind uses the existing is*Response guards instead of
  Object.keys()[0], which reported 'id' for any recorded fixture and
  ignored the audio-first ORDERING CONTRACT in types.ts.
- The dump field holding a kind string is renamed responseKind; on
  Fixture, 'response' already means the response itself.
- The journal's post-filter, pre-pagination total ships as X-Total-Count
  (exposed via CORS). The body stays a bare array for back-compat, so a
  total could never be added to it later.

fix(control-api): resolve chaos scope like getTestId; stop overrides leaking

Five defects in the chaos/inspection control surface, each reproduced against a
running server before the fix and re-run after.

- `LLMock.setChaos()`/`clearChaos()` silently no-opped once an untagged
  `POST /__aimock/chaos` existed: the getter preferred the runtime override
  forever, shadowing `serverOptions.chaos`. They now write through to a running
  server's baseline slot, so the documented in-process API is not dead until the
  next `reset()`.

- `X-Test-Id: ""` on a control call — trivially produced by
  `String(testId ?? "")` — took the untagged branch and installed a SERVER-WIDE
  baseline that failed every other test. A present-but-blank tag is now a 400 on
  GET, POST and DELETE.

- An untagged `DELETE /__aimock/chaos` wiped every per-testId override, so one
  test's cleanup revoked a concurrently-running test's opt-out. Untagged DELETE
  is now symmetric with untagged POST: it drops the baseline only. The baseline
  lives in the same map under DEFAULT_TEST_ID, so "drop the baseline" and "drop
  one test's override" are the same operation and neither can take the other's
  state with it. `POST /__aimock/reset` remains the one full clear.

- Chaos scoping read the `X-Test-Id` header only, while `getTestId` and the
  journal filter also honour `?testId=`: a harness tagging by query param
  installed chaos and watched it do nothing. Both sides now resolve through one
  exported `resolveTestId`, and `applyChaos` takes the raw `req.url` as a
  REQUIRED argument so a new handler cannot forget it.

- `GET /__aimock/fixtures` silently ignored unknown query params while
  `/journal` 400s on them; `?incluide=fixtures` quietly returned the count-only
  body. It now 400s on any param but `include`.

feat(control-api): journal filters, fixtures dump, and runtime chaos control (#435)

## Summary

The `/__aimock/*` control API is documented as the way for harnesses to
manage fixtures/journal/chaos without restarting the server, but it was
missing the read side: `GET /journal` dumped the entire unbounded
journal with no filtering, `GET /fixtures` returned only a count, and
chaos rates were settable only via CLI flags at startup. All three gaps
are closed here — strictly additive, existing responses unchanged when
no new params are used:

- **`GET
/__aimock/journal?limit=&offset=&path=&method=&status=&service=&testId=`**
— filter/paginate the journal (e.g.
`?path=/search&status=200&limit=20`). Invalid `limit/offset/status` →
400. No params → full array, exactly as before.
- **`GET /__aimock/fixtures?include=fixtures`** — `{ count, fixtures: [{
index, match, response, latency?, chaos? }] }` with functions redacted
to `"[function]"` and RegExps stringified, so output is always
JSON-safe. Bare `GET` still returns `{ count }`; unknown `include`
values → 400.
- **`GET /__aimock/chaos` + `PUT /__aimock/chaos`** — read/replace
server-level chaos at runtime (`{dropRate, malformedRate,
disconnectRate}`, each 0–1; `{}` clears). Unknown fields and
out-of-range values → 400. Backed by a new override-aware
`defaults.chaos` getter/setter that still falls through to construction
options until PUT is used. Documented: `POST /reset` does not clear
runtime chaos (PUT `{}` does).

## Verification

- New `src/__tests__/control-inspection.test.ts`: 12 tests — pagination,
every filter, 400 matrix, dump redaction incl. predicate/RegExp
fixtures, chaos read/apply/drop-then-clear cycle, chaos 400 matrix with
nothing-applied assertion.
- No regressions: `control-api` (23), `chaos` (36), `chaos-fixture-mode`
(3), `journal` (40), `server` (64), `llmock` (91).
- `pnpm typecheck`, `eslint`, `prettier` clean.

`VectorMock` is exported, reads request bodies at two entry points of its

Both entry points — the mounted `handleRequest` and the standalone
`start` listener — now answer the same
`400 "Request body must be a JSON object"` the JSON handlers do, placed
immediately after the parse-catch. No `code` (the body parsed, so
`invalid_json` would be inaccurate) and no `param` (a whole-body
rejection names no field). Arrays and scalars are rejected alongside
`null`: every field read as `undefined` and the handlers answered a
misleading `200` on a degenerate empty result.

the malformed-JSON branch keeps its own message.

The AG-UI record/proxy path rebuilt the upstream request instead of
forwarding it. Headers were copied from a hand-picked allowlist of exactly
two names (Authorization, x-api-key) and everything else on the inbound
request was dropped; the body was re-serialized with JSON.stringify over the
parsed input rather than relayed as received.

configuration, and SigV4 material in headers, none of which survived the hop
— and the re-serialization changed key order and whitespace, invalidating a
payload signature even for the headers that did survive.

The proxy now applies the same egress rule the generic recorder proxy already
used: forward everything except hop-by-hop headers, headers the proxy must own
(host, content-length, accept-encoding), cookie, and aimock's own control
headers. Content-Type and Accept are supplied only when the caller did not set
them — overriding a caller-sent header would invalidate a signature computed
over it. The request body is relayed byte-for-byte.

This needs no new configuration. The previous two-header allowlist was never a
deliberate boundary, so restoring transparency is the fix rather than a new
opt-in flag.

proxyAndRecordAGUI now takes the raw request body as a parameter. It is
exported from the package barrel but is not part of the documented API surface
and has no in-tree caller other than AGUIMock.

fix(agui): force Accept upstream and refuse to record a non-SSE response

Review follow-up on the AG-UI proxy passthrough.

Accept was being treated like Content-Type — supplied only when the caller
omitted it. The two are not alike. Content-Type describes the bytes the caller
sent, so the caller owns it and a signature may cover it; Accept describes what
aimock needs back, and AG-UI is an SSE protocol the recorder can only parse as
an event stream. Forwarding a caller's generic Accept (curl's */*, axios's
"application/json, text/plain, */*") let a content-negotiating upstream answer
with JSON, which relayed to the client under a text/event-stream label and
recorded as a zero-event fixture. Accept is now forced. The SigV4 rationale
does not reach it: AWS signs host, content-type and the x-amz-* family, and
accept is not in SignedHeaders.

The recorder also now refuses to build a fixture when a 2xx upstream answers
with a non-event-stream Content-Type, or with a stream that yields no parseable
AG-UI events. Both used to persist "events": [] — a fixture that then MATCHED
on replay and streamed nothing, with no fixture-miss log and no parse warning,
so the failure surfaced only as a silently empty agent turn. The response is
still relayed to the client in full; only the recording is skipped, and it says
why. That hole predates the passthrough change but the passthrough is what made
it reachable.

rawBody moves to the last parameter of proxyAndRecordAGUI. It is a barrel
export, and in the 4th position a JavaScript caller written against the old
signature would have silently passed `fixtures` as the request body. In last
position such a call leaves it undefined, which is now rejected before an
upstream connection is opened.

Also: a CHANGELOG entry under [Unreleased], the aimock-internal header families
(x-aimock-strict, x-aimock-context, x-aimock-chaos-*) added to the strip test,
and the docs page corrected to describe forcing rather than defaulting Accept.

fix(agui): forward inbound headers and raw body through the record proxy (#455)

## The problem

`enableRecording({ upstream })` rebuilt the upstream request instead of
forwarding it.

1. **Headers.** `proxyAndRecordAGUI` constructed a fresh header object
containing `Content-Type`, `Accept`, and — if present — `Authorization`
and `x-api-key`. Every other inbound header was dropped.
2. **Body.** The payload was re-serialized with `JSON.stringify(input)`
from the parsed object rather than relayed as it arrived.

Reported by a customer running their agent on AWS Bedrock AgentCore,
where the runtime contract lives in headers: session affinity,
per-request agent configuration, and SigV4 material. None of it survived
the hop. The re-serialization independently invalidated the payload
signature by changing key order and whitespace.

Verified against 1.39.0 and still present on `main`. In a proxy-only
repro, of eight headers sent the upstream received only `content-type`,
`accept`, `authorization`, `x-api-key`, `content-length`, `host`, and
`connection`.

## The fix

The AG-UI proxy now applies the same egress rule the generic recorder
proxy has always used — `buildForwardHeaders`, already in `recorder.ts`:

- Forward every inbound header except hop-by-hop ones (`connection`,
`keep-alive`, `transfer-encoding`, `te`, `trailer`, `upgrade`,
`proxy-authorization`, `proxy-authenticate` — named exactly, so
`proxy-connection` is *not* stripped), headers the proxy must own
(`host`, `content-length`, `accept-encoding`), `cookie`, and aimock's
own control headers (`x-test-id`, `x-aimock-strict`, `x-aimock-context`,
and the `x-aimock-chaos-*` prefix).
- Supply `Content-Type` **only when the caller did not set it**. The
caller owns it — it describes the bytes they sent — and overriding it
would invalidate a signature computed over it, since SigV4 and friends
sign a named subset of headers. This is what the new
`setForwardHeaderDefault` helper enforces.
- **Force `Accept` to `text/event-stream`.** Unlike `Content-Type`,
`Accept` describes what aimock needs back, and AG-UI is an SSE protocol
the recorder can only parse as an event stream. Forwarding a caller's
generic `*/*` lets a content-negotiating upstream answer with JSON.
`accept` is not in SigV4's `SignedHeaders`, so forcing it is safe where
forcing `Content-Type` would not be.
- Relay the request body byte-for-byte. `proxyAndRecordAGUI` takes the
raw payload; `input` stays the parsed view used for fixture matching
only.

### Why no new configuration

The customer asked for two opt-in options (`forwardHeaders`, `rawBody`)
with defaults unchanged. The cleaner answer is neither.

The two-header allowlist was never a deliberate boundary — a proxy that
silently drops what it has not heard of is the bug, and the rest of this
codebase already agreed, since the generic proxy path forwards
transparently. Re-serializing the body is likewise never more correct
than relaying it. So this restores transparency in the default path
instead of adding two knobs to opt back into correct behavior, and the
AG-UI path now matches the generic one rather than diverging from it.

Header-sensitive integrations work with no config change.

## Recording refusal

A 2xx upstream that answers with a non-event-stream `Content-Type`, or
with a stream yielding no parseable events, is no longer recorded. Both
previously persisted `"events": []` — a fixture that then **matched** on
replay and streamed nothing, with no fixture-miss log and no parse
warning, so the failure surfaced only as a silently empty agent turn.
The response is still relayed to the client in full; only the recording
is skipped, and it logs why. The hole predates this PR; forwarding the
caller's headers is what made it reachable.

## API surface

`proxyAndRecordAGUI` gains a required `rawBody` parameter, appended
**last**. In an earlier position a JavaScript caller written against the
old signature would have silently passed `fixtures` as the request body;
last, such a call leaves it `undefined`, which is rejected before an
upstream connection is opened. It is exported from the package barrel
but is not part of the documented API surface and has no in-tree caller
other than `AGUIMock`.

## Tests

New `src/__tests__/agui-proxy-passthrough.test.ts` runs the real proxy
path against a capturing upstream:

- arbitrary inbound headers (session id, agent config, custom tenant)
reach the upstream
- the body arrives byte-for-byte, including non-canonical key order,
whitespace, and unrecognized fields, with a matching `content-length`
- caller-set `Content-Type` / `Accept` are not overridden
- the defaults are supplied when the caller omits them
- caller-set `Accept` is overridden with `text/event-stream`
- hop-by-hop, `cookie`, `accept-encoding`, `x-test-id`,
`x-aimock-strict`, `x-aimock-context` and `x-aimock-chaos-*` are
stripped, and `host` is the target's
- a 2xx non-event-stream upstream is relayed but not recorded, and says
why
- an event stream with no parseable events is likewise relayed but not
recorded

Six of the eight fail without their corresponding fix; the other two are
regression guards on behavior that was already correct.

`src/__tests__/drift/bedrock-stream.drift.ts` is the only file emitting
drift results for `bedrock-invoke`, `bedrock-invoke-stream`,
`bedrock-converse` and `bedrock-converse-stream`. It was
`describe.skipIf(!AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID && !AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY &&
!AWS_REGION)` — and none of those three appear anywhere in
`.github/workflows/test-drift.yml`. Six cases, never executed in CI.
`vertex-ai.drift.ts` is the same shape on
`GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` / `VERTEX_AI_PROJECT`: two more cases,
never executed.

Neither file needs credentials. Nothing in this repo implements AWS
SigV4 signing or a GCP OAuth2 token exchange, so both only ever drive
the local aimock server. A credential gate guarded tests that need no
credentials, and five surfaces reported as covered while nothing looked
at them.

## How a surface got marked "covered"

`SURFACE_REGISTRY` membership, and nothing else.
`drift-collector.test.ts` enforces registry ⟺ emitter bidirectionally,
so an entry means "some `formatDriftReport(…, slug)` call site exists" —
it cannot distinguish a surface graded against the **vendor** from one
graded against a **fixture in this repo**. Scanning the emitting
sources, **9 of 27** surfaces are mock-only, not 5.

## What changed

- `SurfaceMapping` gains a **required** `liveCoverage: "live" | "none"`,
with no default — omission used to imply coverage. `coverageNote` is
required by the type on `"none"`.
- `drift-report.json` carries **`unverifiedSurfaces`** on every run,
written even when empty so a missing field means "an old report", never
"everything was verified". The collector prints the list, and the
clean-run line now reads `No critical diffs found (on the surfaces that
were actually checked — 9 surface(s) have no live coverage at all).`
- `drift-collector.test.ts` **re-derives** live-capability from the
emitting `*.drift.ts` sources (import of
`providers.js`/`ws-providers.js`, or a request whose target is not the
local mock). A declaration that contradicts the code fails CI in
**both** directions, plus an explicit roster so deleting a surface to
shorten the list is also caught.
- Both credential gates removed. The cases run unconditionally as
offline conformance.
- `DRIFT.md` documents live coverage vs offline conformance under
"Reading Results".

## On the "tautology"

`triangulate(sdkShape, sdkShape, mockShape)` is **not** vacuous, and I
did not delete the assertions. `triangulate`'s `sdk`/`real`/`mock` legs
are three separate inputs; with `real === sdk` the `LLMOCK DRIFT — field
in SDK + real API but missing from mock` and `TYPE MISMATCH between real
API and mock` branches both still fire at `critical`. What the
duplication kills is the `SDK STALE` / `PROVIDER ADDED FIELD` branches —
the ones that need a real observation. So these are genuine
mock-vs-fixture conformance checks that grade nothing about the vendor,
which is exactly what the `liveCoverage: "none"` declaration now says.

## Two real bugs the gate was hiding

The first run with the gates removed was **red**, 2 of 8:

```

     Path: body          Mock: <absent>

     Path: $metadata     Mock: <absent>

mock and serves the wire body, so those three fields could never be
present.

delegates to **`anthropicMessageShape()`** — the same fixture the LIVE
Anthropic drift leg grades `api.anthropic.com` against every run, so the
expected shape stays tethered to an observation of a real provider — and
`$metadata` is gone from the Converse fixture. Verified against the

## What

`POST /v1/images/variations` only ever served `dall-e-2`. OpenAI removed
`dall-e-2` on 2026-05-12 and removed the endpoint with it. aimock still
answered the path with a **200 image envelope** — mocking success for a
surface that no longer serves. #459 refreshed the image defaults and
left variations defaulting to `gpt-image-1`, a model that endpoint never
supported, so the default was wrong in a new way on top of a dead route.

Per the [deprecation
policy](https://aimock.copilotkit.dev/deprecation-policy/) rule 2, a
removed surface is **mocked as removed**: the route stays registered and
replays the rejection the live API returns today, so the removal
surfaces in the caller's tests instead of in production.

**This is a consumer-visible behaviour change.** Anyone whose tests
drive `/v1/images/variations` will now see a 404 instead of an image.

## Provenance — every wire value was observed, none invented

The critical question was whether the *endpoint* is gone or whether it
still exists and rejects `dall-e-2` as an invalid model. Those need
different mocks. It is the former, established two ways.

**Keyless routing probe** (a removed endpoint 404s before auth; a live
endpoint 401s):

```
POST /v1/images/generations   -> HTTP/2 401   {"message":"Missing bearer or basic authentication in header", ...}
POST /v1/images/edits         -> HTTP/2 401
POST /v1/images/variations    -> HTTP/2 404   <- 404s BEFORE auth
POST /v1/images/bogus         -> HTTP/2 404   <- a made-up path: identical
POST /v1/chat/completions     -> HTTP/2 401
```

**Authenticated probe**, 2026-09-15, live key resolved through
`internal-skills secret-cache` (never on argv, never printed, never
persisted), multipart with `model=dall-e-2`:

```
POST /v1/images/variations
HTTP/2 404
cf-cache-status: DYNAMIC
server: cloudflare
  http=404 size=0 ctype=[]        <- ZERO-byte body, NO content-type

POST /v1/images/bogus            -> HTTP/2 404, identical header set
OPTIONS /v1/images/variations    -> HTTP/2 404

CONTROL, same key, same session:
POST /v1/images/generations -> HTTP/2 400  openai-version: 2020-10-01  openai-organization: tawkit  x-request-id: req_cafab...
POST /v1/images/edits       -> HTTP/2 400  openai-version: 2020-10-01  x-request-id: req_d3413...
```

**The verbatim error body is the empty string.** The variations 404
carries no `openai-version`, no `x-request-id`, no `openai-organization`
and no body at all — it is a CDN-edge 404 that never reaches the OpenAI
application, whereas `generations` and `edits` demonstrably do. A live
endpoint rejecting a dead model would have returned an app-level JSON
`invalid_request_error`. There is no JSON envelope to replay because the
real API sends none, so the mock must not invent one.

**Labelled inferred, not observed:** the *causal* link to the 2026-05-12
`dall-e-2` removal is inferred from the timeline and from the fact that
`dall-e-2` was the endpoint's only supported model. What is observed is
only that the path 404s today. `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` on aimock's
own reply is a Node artifact of ending a response with no body, not an
authored wire value.

**One deliberate departure from the capture:** aimock still sets its own
CORS headers on the 404 (the CDN 404 carries none), so a browser-based
caller sees the 404 rather than a CORS failure masking it. Status, empty
body and absent `Content-Type` are exactly as observed.

`readBody` decoded every request body to a utf8 string, which corrupts

  text path is byte-identical to before (same `Buffer.concat` + `toString`),

  counted, so the route still sees `end` and can answer a real 400 with
  headers; past `drainMaxBytes` the socket is dropped exactly as before.

fix(files): make the Files API mock strict, byte-exact and consistent

Upload parsing (JSON and multipart share one rule set):

- Accept the create-purpose enum (`assistants`, `batch`, `fine-tune`,
  `vision`, `user_data`, `evals`) and name the accepted values in the 400.
- Reject malformed bodies instead of coercing or fabricating: the JSON body
  must be valid UTF-8, exactly one of `content`/`bytes` must be present, and
  no field is `String()`-coerced or defaulted.
- One `filenameError` for both parsers: no control characters, no unpaired
  UTF-16 surrogate, at most 1024 UTF-8 bytes (a longer name makes the
  Content-Disposition header on the content route unsendable).
- Frame multipart per RFC 2046 §5.1.1 rather than splitting on the boundary
  token, so a payload that contains the boundary is stored whole. Reject
  duplicate or ambiguous part headers, parts that declare a non-identity
  Content-Transfer-Encoding / Content-Encoding, and anything other than
  exactly one payload part (`file`, or its `content` alias).
- A filename-less multipart part gets a name derived from the content hash,
  not the clock, so repeated uploads are deterministic.
- Copy the payload into its own Buffer so the store owns the bytes rather
  than holding a view of the whole request body.

Size caps:

- `FILES_BODY_MAX_BYTES` (content cap plus worst-case wire expansion and
  envelope headroom) and `FILES_BODY_DRAIN_MAX_BYTES` let the route answer
  an over-size upload with a 400 via the `FILES_BODY_OVERSIZED` sentinel,
  instead of the socket being dropped before the cap check could run.

Storage and reads:

- Store contents as `Buffer`s, never round-tripped through a utf8 string,
  so binary uploads come back byte-for-byte identical.
- The content route derives Content-Type from the stored filename's
  extension (never from the client-declared part header), sets
  Content-Length, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, and an RFC 5987
  `Content-Disposition: attachment` with a UTF-8 `filename*` fallback.
- List reads `limit`, `after`, `order` and `purpose` itself under one rule:
  a repeated parameter is a 400, `limit` is a strict decimal integer within
  `[1, 10000]`, `order` is `asc`/`desc`, `after` must name an existing file,
  and a literal `#` in a value is part of the value.

- Switch every handler to `applyChaosAsync` so configured latency delays
  Files responses like every other route, tag the chaos-path journal entry
  with `service: "files"`, and set CORS headers before the chaos gate so a
  faulted response is readable from a browser.

The store deliberately does not FIFO-evict: files are durable objects the
real API keeps until deleted, and the module header documents that

fix(chaos): parse every chaos input through one field table and reject instead of clamping

Header, fixture and server-default chaos values each had their own hand-written
parser and bounds, and all of them clamped: a rate of 5 quietly became 1.0, a
latency of 90000 became 30000, and parseFloat took the numeric prefix out of

most a warning that said "clamping".

Introduce CHAOS_FIELDS as the single table of chaos fields (header spelling,
upper bound, integer-vs-rate grammar) and parseChaosNumber/parseChaosField as
the one parser every source goes through. Values are now REJECTED, never
clamped: out-of-range, non-finite, negative zero, fractional milliseconds, and
any string that is not a plain decimal (hex, binary, exponent, Infinity, a sign,
trailing garbage) are refused and left unset so the next level of precedence
(header > fixture > server) applies. Repeated headers, in both the array and
comma-folded shapes Node produces, take the first non-empty value and warn once
when the values disagree by meaning rather than by spelling.

Rejections are reported honestly: per-request headers warn every time (dynamic
input), while static fixture/server values are latched once per distinct
source+field+value, per server (a WeakMap keyed by the server's Logger, capped
at 64 keys) so one typo does not print on every request and two servers in one
process do not share a latch. The warning names the specific fixture via
describeMatch, which moves from router.ts into helpers.ts so both call sites

The sync applyChaos() cannot await, so every handler that called it rolled the
fault dice but silently skipped the configured latencyMs. Route every provider

messages, ollama, openrouter, responses, speech, transcription, veo, video)

so headers are parsed (and warned about) once instead of twice.

afterwards is not blamed on the client), client-gone, and headers-sent. Only the

that need their own status line, so disconnect still applies and the latency is

applyChaosAsync returns a ChaosAsyncOutcome (false | "handled" | "unwritable")
so callers can tell "an action fired and was journalled" from "the response was
already dead"; both non-false members stay truthy so the usual
`if (await applyChaosAsync(...)) return;` is unchanged. applyChaosAction returns
"applied" | "skipped" and does nothing at all (no write, no journal entry, no
metric) when the response cannot take that action; the aimock_chaos_triggered_total
counter is incremented after the write so a throwing write leaves no metric
behind. It now requires a logger argument so a skip is never invisible.

The chaos 429 goes through writeErrorResponse so it carries the same OpenAI-shaped
rate-limit header set as every other 429 in the repo.

fal requests were double-rolled: the server gate rolled unconditionally and the
legacy /fal/queue and /fal/run routes rolled again on passthrough (a configured
0.5 drop rate measured ~0.72). falWillHandle predicts handleFal's passthrough
decision from the same classification, so the server gate rolls only when it owns
the request. Un-fixtured fal chaos is journalled as source "internal", not
"fixture".

The public barrel keeps exporting applyChaos (published since v1.10.0) but binds
it to applyChaosDeprecated, which warns once per process that the sync form skips

fix(chaos): validate control-API and CLI chaos fields through the shared table

POST /__aimock/chaos re-typed its own field list and bounds, and the --chaos-*
CLI flags re-typed theirs again, so the three entry points could disagree. They
did: the control API accepted `{ latencyMs: 250.5 }` with a 200 and echoed it from
GET, while the resolver discarded it at request time as a non-integer, reporting
a config the traffic never saw.

so raising a cap in the one table moves the endpoint and the flags with it. The
control API still requires JSON numbers (a numeric string is a client-side type
error, not a wire spelling); the CLI reads --chaos-* text through the same
plain-decimal grammar as the headers, and the --help text derives the latency
cap from the table.

Installing a scoped override REPLACES the config for that testId; it is not
merged over the baseline. The endpoint documents that contract, and it names
every field that was in effect for the scope and is not restated (for example a
server-wide --chaos-latency vanishing under a scoped `{ dropRate: 1 }`) in a
warning so a dropped baseline rate is never silent. GET /__aimock/chaos selects
the scope with `has`, matching the resolver, so an installed-but-empty override
reports as "no chaos" rather than falling back to the baseline it shadows.

POST /__aimock/reset clears the server's chaos warning latch alongside the
runtime chaos override, so a suite that resets between tests sees a bad static
chaos value reported again.

fix(fixtures): carry cross-file validation refs as data and keep the loader a text file

Two `validateFixtures` rules -- `duplicate userMessage` and the catch-all
ordering check -- name OTHER fixtures in the array they were given, so their
message text embeds an index. `aimock validate` runs the rules per file and
then over the union of every file, and has to renumber those indices for the
reader. Rewriting the rendered prose with a regex is unsafe: `duplicate
userMessage` interpolates the fixture's own `userMessage`, so user-authored
text that happens to read "fixture 3" would be corrupted.

Each such finding now carries a `ref` (`ValidationRef`) with the rule name and
the raw indices, and `renderValidationRef` renders the message from it. With
`String` it reproduces the exact message `validateFixtures` emitted before, so
existing consumers see no change; the CLI passes a renderer that resolves a
union index to `<file> #<index-in-that-file>`. Both `ValidationRef` and
`renderValidationRef` are exported from the package entry.

`serializeMatcher` joined a RegExp's source and flags with a literal U+0000
byte, which made `src/fixture-loader.ts` a binary file for git, grep and
diff. The separator is now the backslash-u0000 escape -- same runtime string, so
`/ag/i` and `/a/gi` still get distinct dedup keys, and a test pins that.

fix(cli): rework aimock validate to walk directories, contain failures, and report one run

`aimock validate` now accepts fixture files or directories. A directory is
walked recursively for `*.json` in the order `--fixtures <dir>` loads it,
following symlinks the way the server does but reporting a directory symlink
that points back into the walk once, as a cycle, instead of recursing to
ELOOP. A `*.json` path that is not a regular file is a per-file error rather
than a blocking read. Paths are compared by resolved path, so a path
mentioned twice -- or reached once directly and once through a symlink -- is
several loads of the same file, numbered `<path>[<n>]` on every rendering
surface (human lines, summary, cross-file references, and a `mention` field
on each `--json` `files[]` entry) so a duplicate never reads as a fixture
shadowing itself.

Files are classified before they are converted. A file the caller names must
be a `{ "fixtures": [...] }` envelope and fails otherwise. A file the WALK
turns up that parses but has no top-level `fixtures` key is not a fixture
file -- this package's own `fixtures/` tree holds aimock configs next to
fixtures -- and is skipped with a note, naming an aimock config for what it
is; a walked file whose `fixtures` key is present but not an array fails.
Each entry is checked for shape before `entryToFixture` runs, and an entry
whose `match` is a scalar or array (which converts to an empty catch-all on
both sides) is a warning that `--strict` promotes.

`validateFixtures` runs once per file for attribution and once over the
union of every parsed file, in load order, so the cross-file rules fire; the
union pass adds only the findings the per-file pass could not see, rendered
from ref data via `renderValidationRef` rather than by regex over the text.
Per-entry conversion warnings the server logs are collected and surfaced
instead of dropped.

Nothing escapes the run: an unreadable path, a stat failure, a malformed
entry or a crash inside either rules pass becomes a per-file or run-level
error in the report, which is still emitted -- as valid JSON under `--json`
-- and still exits 1. Run-level errors print after the per-file output, and
"no fixtures loaded" is withheld when a file already said why it loaded none.
Human and `--json` mode report the same facts, a fatal file counting as one
record in both. `--json` keeps stdout to exactly one JSON document, including
for `--help`, `--json=true` and a usage error; everything that fails the run
goes to stderr. A remote source (`https://...`) is refused as unsupported
rather than read as a filename. `--` stops option parsing, an empty option
value is a usage error, `-h` is `--help`, and a usage error exits 1 like
every other CLI surface in this package. The help text states what the lint
actually checks and how it differs from the server's `--validate-on-load`.

fix(cli): make -h mean --help, refuse blank option values, and run the compiled CJS entry

A short flag now means the same thing at the top level and in every
subcommand of the `aimock` bin: `-h` is `--help`, as `convert` and `validate`
already had it, and the host override is long-form `--host` only. Before,
`aimock -h` silently consumed the next argument as a bind address. The
separate `llmock` bin (the Docker entrypoint) keeps its own documented set.

A value-taking option that was GIVEN an empty or blank value is a usage error
naming the option, not an absent option. Truthiness checks let `--config ""`
read as "not given" and dropped `--port ""` / `--host ""` in silence;
`--host ""` reached the server as an empty bind address, which listens on
every interface instead of the documented 127.0.0.1.

The entry-point guard lists `aimock-cli.cjs` alongside `aimock-cli.js`:
tsdown builds both formats and `node dist/aimock-cli.cjs` printed nothing and
exited 0 despite its shebang and exec bit.

The top-level synopsis shows `aimock validate [--strict] [--json] [--] <path>
[more paths ...]`, so the first help a user sees carries the `--` terminator
and says validate takes directories. The aimock-cli suite pins each of these,
including the CJS entry and that the synopsis matches the README verbatim.

test(cli): cover aimock validate end to end and pin the vitest pool

fix(observability): make the journal, metrics and one-shot error injection report what happened (#466)

This PR aligns the request journal and Prometheus metrics with the
response actually delivered, and makes one-shot error injection safe
across concurrent requests. A handler crash amends its own request
entry; a destroyed socket is recorded as interrupted rather than as a
delivered error. Compatible requests reserve a queued error before
asynchronous chaos processing, and release it if it is never served.

## Behavior

### Journal and route errors

- Route catches share error handling for logging, CORS, error envelopes,
and journaling. Entries are attributed by server request identity
through `AsyncLocalStorage` and `Journal.onAdd`, so concurrent requests
sharing an `x-request-id` cannot amend each other's entries.
- A crash after a completed response preserves the delivered status and
adds `response.error`. A crash during a response marks it interrupted;
SSE crashes emit their error frame and destroy the socket. Proxy
interruption reasons distinguish a client disconnect from recorder
destruction.
- Files, batches, fine-tuning, and ElevenLabs voice catches retain
service attribution. Files and voice journal after successful response
writes, avoiding phantom entries when writes throw; files errors include
their envelopes, and voice entries carry `service: "elevenlabs-voice"`.
- Body-size enforcement destroys the request socket. Those requests now
log at warn and journal `status: 0`, `interrupted: true`, and
`interruptReason: "request body exceeded size limit"`, without
attempting a response on the dead transport. Metrics count `destroyed`.
Deliverable malformed JSON still receives and journals 400. Client
aborts similarly record an interruption with reason `client aborted`.
- Files rejection warnings escape control characters and Unicode line
separators and cap the complete warning to 1,024 characters before the
logger prefix. Request-controlled purpose/cursor text cannot forge
another log line or generate request-sized warnings. Response and
journal envelopes retain their existing contents and limits.

### One-shot errors and chaos

- `LLMock.nextRequestError` and `POST /__aimock/error` share the
existing endpoint-compatibility rule and queue. Selection reserves the
one-shot before awaiting chaos in chat, embeddings, and all four
ElevenLabs voice routes, including mixed chat/embedding concurrency.
Exactly one request receives the injected error.
- Unserved reservations return to the queue after chaos or cancellation.
Queue clearing/reset/hot reload advances a generation so an older
request cannot restore an error into a reset queue. OpenRouter fallback
cannot consume an error while discarding its candidate; queued errors
appear as `responseKind: "error"` in the control API.
- Chaos source labels use one provider-aware proxy rule, including
per-request strict mode. A strict malformed response is applied locally
and labeled `internal`; unrelated upstream configuration cannot label a
locally answered request `proxy`.
- Chaos journaling follows writes, preserves committed status for
disconnects, and records null request bodies for fal gates where
appropriate. All five fixture chaos fields and server defaults use the
shared validation table, rejecting invalid rates, non-finite values,
negative zero, strings, and fractional latency consistently.

### Metrics and library semantics

- Metrics count both completed and destroyed responses once, and retain
malformed-Host requests under `{unknown}`. Labels follow route shape
independently of response status, preserving routed fixture-miss 404s
while bounding unknown paths.
- Dynamic Gemini/Vertex actions, fal paths, music paths, and
files/batches depths use bounded labels. Control and mount labels take
precedence over provider patterns, matching dispatch order, including
mounts beneath `/fal`, `/v1/files`, and `/v1/music`. Mounts added after
startup are read at record time; overlapping mounts retain registration
order. Bare `/fal` shares the router's path rule.
- `Journal.getAll` returns nothing for finite nonpositive limits, floors
fractions, and treats non-finite values as unlimited. Journal test-id
filtering shares the full-header resolver used for request scoping.
- `clearRequests()` preserves fixture match counts; sibling sequencing
compares `toolResultContains` and `context`. Fixture debug descriptions
render predicates and nested objects more readably.

  chunk (#470)
- Journals and metrics reflect delivered vs interrupted responses; one-shot errors never
  double-deliver (#466)

  provider (#467)
- AG-UI drift reads generated 1.0 schemas; `AGUIRunStartedEvent` gains optional `protocolVersion`
  (#469)
- Drift reports list `unverifiedSurfaces`; offline Bedrock/Vertex checks no longer skip silently
  (#460)
- Drift docs match actual coverage; ElevenLabs drift separates vendor observations from fixture
  checks (#465)
- Chaos no longer treats committed headers as a dead response; only status-writing actions are
  skipped (#449)
- Chaos skip logs name what happened; `aimock_chaos_triggered_total` counts only written responses
  (#449)
- A request whose chaos latency was cancelled by client hang-up is no longer served or journalled
  (#449)
- Moderations echoes the request's `model`; default is now `omni-moderation-latest` (#459)
- Image endpoints default to `gpt-image-1` — `dall-e-2`/`dall-e-3` were removed (#459)
- AG-UI record/proxy forwards the caller's headers and raw body upstream; `Accept` is forced to SSE
  (#455)
- The AG-UI recorder refuses to write a fixture from a non-stream or empty 2xx upstream reply (#455)
- A MINTED `x-request-id` is no longer forwarded upstream in record/proxy mode (#450)
